blocks.text: Light is defined as a form of electromagnetic radiation, specifically the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that is visible to the human eye.
Light has dual nature (Light exhibits both wave-like and particle-like characteristics).
Light can also be described as a stream of particles called photons, which carry energy.
Light travels at a constant speed in a vacuum, approx.
Light is a form of transverse wave that travels in vacuum.
Light can be polarized.
Young's Double-Slit Experiment
It was performed in 1801 by Thomas Young, demonstrates the wave-like nature of light, showing that light can interfere with itself, creating an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes.
The photoelectric effect is a phenomenon where electrons are emitted from the metal surface when light of sufficient frequency is incident upon it.
This effect led to the conclusion that light is made up of packets or quanta of energy.
Heinrich Rudolf Hertz was the first to observe the photoelectric effect in 1887.

_ Photoelectron proposed the existence of photons, packets discrete Melal Surface of energy, to explain the Photoelectric effect and other light-related phenomena (received Nobel Prize in 1921).
Reflection occurs when light rays strike a surface and change direction, returning to the same medium instead of Passing through or being absorbed.
Laws of Reflection 1. The angle of incidence (i) is equal to the angle of reflection (r).
2. The incident ray, reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.

The refraction of light is the bending of light rays as they pass from one medium to another, thereby causing a change in its speed and direction. Refraction occurs due to a change in the speed of the light ray or wave.
While the speed and wavelength of light changes as it moves into a different medium, the frequency, which is determined by the light source, remains constant.

Laws of Refraction 1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence: All lie in the same plane.
2. The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence (i) and sine of the angle of refraction (r) is constant (also known as Snell's Law).

Types of Media 1. Rarer Medium: Light bends away from the normal when moving from a denser to a rarer medium.
2. Denser Medium: Light bends toward the normal when moving from a rarer to a denser medium.
Let's Take a Look At Three Cases
Case A: Same Medium (No Refraction)
When light travels through two media with the same optical density (E.g., air to air or water to water), it continues in a straight line without bending.
This is because the speed of light remains constant, and there's no change in the direction of the light ray.
Case B: From Rarer to Denser Medium
When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium (E.g., air to glass or water), it bends towards the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence).
Zi is greater than Zr.
The speed of light decreases in the denser medium.
Case C: From Denser to Rarer Medium eWhen light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium (e.g., glass to air), it bends away from the normal.
Zi is less than Zr.
The speed of light increases in the rarer medium.
